risk_flags.description: The diagnosis '乙肝肝硬化' (hepatitis B cirrhosis) is stated in the history, but there is no supporting evidence in the chart (e.g., imaging, labs, biopsy).

specialist_trace.rationale: To ensure accurate coding, the documentation must specify the underlying cause of the bleeding as esophageal variceal rupture (e.g., “esophageal variceal bleeding due to portal hypertension”) rather than the generic “upper GI bleeding,” and explicitly state the severity (e.g., “severe acute variceal hemorrhage with hemodynamic instability”) based on the hypotension and tachycardia. Additionally, clarify whether this is an initial or recurrent episode of variceal bleeding, and document the chronic liver disease (hepatitis B cirrhosis) as a coexisting condition, as this directly impacts the clinical picture and coding specificity.

The chart's diagnosis of "upper gastrointestinal bleeding" is correct but insufficiently specific; literature supports that in cirrhotic patients with hematemesis, esophageal variceal bleeding is the most common and life-threatening etiology, and endoscopy-confirmed variceal bleeding should be explicitly coded as such (PMID: 31647287). The hemodynamic parameters (HR 110, BP 95/60, Hb 75) indicate moderate-to-severe bleeding per Baveno VII criteria, which recommend risk stratification (e.g., AIMS65, Rockall) and urgent management—this severity should be documented to guide resuscitation and early TIPS consideration (PMID: 34853061). Regarding temporal aspect, recurrent variceal bleeding carries a higher 6-week mortality (~20%) than first episodes, so the chart should clarify whether this is an index bleed or rebleeding to adjust secondary prophylaxis and surveillance intervals (PMID: 32282032).
